drafted_from: tool:issue-a-tls-certificate's row in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/tool-rows.json, do-work/renew-a-tls-certificate.mjs, do-work/tls-host-owner.py and the tests in test/
start_here: Say to your AI: "Issue a certificate for app.example.com on my server at 192.0.2.34, reached as admin with its pinned key." It runs tool:issue-a-tls-certificate with your DNS key and keeps a still-valid certificate instead of replacing it.
no_lists_because: It keeps no list of its own: it takes one server's facts as its input and answers what that server's certificate owner reports.
instructions: 1. Gather the server's facts: its public name, IPv4 address, SSH port, the administrator you sign in as, its pinned key ("<address> ssh-ed25519 <key>") and its layout (host: owner path, state folder, downloads folder, ingress, receptionist). The README in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/ shows a made-up one.

2. Say to your AI the sentence in start_here. It calls run_resource_operation at @workshop-tools with method tools:run, tool tool:issue-a-tls-certificate and that input (the worked example shows one). The door mounts your server administration key for the run; you paste no key.

3. Read what comes back: the certificate as the server verified it, preexisting_dns_records_unchanged, certificate_changed and dry_run (false). An {"error": ...} or a thrown message names what to change (for example the layout or the pinned key was refused).
4. Next run tool:write-a-public-hosts-paths and tool:switch-on-a-servers-receptionist; renewals later go through tool:renew-a-tls-certificate.
